source.title: Safety Arithmetic: A Framework for Test-time Safety Alignment of Language Models by Steering Parameters and Activations
source.authors: Rima Hazra; Sayan Layek; Somnath Banerjee; Soujanya Poria

record.tranche_reason: The paper applies the named ORTHO jailbreak attack and reports its harmful-response success rate, including when combined with other interventions. This is a conceptual test of V3's attack component, not a reproduction of the original residual-stream ablation experiment.
record.gate_note: Rows are limited to the paper's own ORTHO attack results in Tables 9 and 10. The main Safety Arithmetic, HDR, and Safe-Align results use a parameter-space harm vector or an in-context safety vector, not the original harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction, so their safety and utility metrics are not rows for these claim versions. The text identifies ORTHO as an attack but does not describe its mechanism; the rows report attack outcomes, not independent evidence that direction suppression caused them.
record.test_reason: Appendix A.4 applies ORTHO, the weight-orthogonalization edit from the original source (Arditi et al. 2024), to released llama2-7b-chat-hf. It reports harmful-response ASR on DangerousQA and HarmBench. This bears on V2 (weight-edit removal of refusal in a released model), not V3: nothing about jailbreak mechanisms or training against ablation is studied. The intervention and model match the original. The judge (GPT-4) and prompt differ, and the ORTHO implementation details are not given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right for the appendix: the authors say ORTHO 'can indeed jailbreak' Safety-Aligned models, and adding Safe-Align lowers its ASR, showing the need for test-time safety. Their main conclusion is that Safety Arithmetic (HDR plus Safe-Align) cuts ASR across base, fine-tuned and edited models while keeping utility and reducing over-safety.
record.recipe_differences: The paper's own safety method subtracts a pruned parameter-space harm vector derived from fine-tuning, then adds an activation-space in-context safety vector. It does not reproduce the original residual-stream difference-in-means direction intervention. It also evaluates the separately named ORTHO attack.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported ORTHO ASR varies by evaluation dataset and by whether HDR and Safe-Align are combined with the attack.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding an activation steering vector reduces ASR on Llama2, Mistral and fine-tuned models (Tables 1-3). The vector is the first principal direction of safe-minus-unsafe answer-pair representations (Safe-Align ICV). It also partly counters ORTHO (10.5% to 8% on DangerousQA; 26.41% to 19.49% on HarmBench).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A safety direction from paired safe/unsafe responses, added at inference, lowers harmful compliance and partly restores safety after refusal-direction orthogonalization.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: For the ORTHO results, no uncertainty estimates are reported. The text does not describe the ORTHO mechanism or establish that its outcomes are caused by suppressing the refusal direction. The Safe-Align-plus-ORTHO table condition is described inconsistently: the setting label includes HDR, while the prose describes applying ORTHO after HDR and then Safe-Align.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's own Safety Arithmetic/HDR/Safe-Align safety-rate results, utility benchmarks, and over-safety rates were left out because they evaluate interventions different from the claim's original residual-stream direction. No additional ORTHO result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Capability retention after ORTHO; other released models (e.g. Mistral); the direction extraction and layer choice used for ORTHO.
Activation-level ablation or addition of the difference-in-means direction.
Whether jailbreaks act by suppressing the direction; adversarial training against ablation.

missing.what: Unedited llama2-7b-chat-hf HarmBench ASR, needed as the baseline for ORTHO's 26.41%
Original-model DangerousQA ASR (8.50%) as the baseline for the ORTHO row

record.verdict_notes: The reader misread ORTHO as a V3 jailbreak result; it is the original paper's weight orthogonalization, i.e. V2. ORTHO is only an appendix comparison, with no description of how the direction or layer was chosen, and no uncertainty. The paper's 'harm direction' (HDR) is a parameter-space task vector from harmful fine-tuning, not the refusal direction.

versions.untested_parts: The difference-in-means residual direction, its ablation or addition, and the effect on general capability under those interventions.
Weight-edit removal of the original refusal direction in released models.
Whether the reported ORTHO results arise specifically from suppressing the direction; training against its ablation and the resulting robustness.
Whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or involves multiple directions.
Whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are separately encoded.
Transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Whether refusal-training choices determine the existence of a removable direction.
Whether V1 holds in reasoning models.

relation.reason: The study's own appendix results (Tables 9-10) measure how far the weight edit raises harmful compliance in a released chat model. That bears directly on V2.

tranche.reason: Appendix A.4 applies ORTHO, cited to Arditi et al. 2024, to llama2-7b-chat-hf and reports HarmBench ASR. That is the original's weight-edit method and benchmark. It is a loose T1: the judge is GPT-4 rather than the HarmBench classifier, the authors add DangerousQA, and they describe no implementation details. A T3 reading would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: r1's baseline should be 8.50% (Table 1). DangerousQA has about 200 questions, so the 2-point rise is about 4 questions. This is a small appendix side-experiment with no ORTHO details, HarmBench subset size or system prompt. Its 26.41% HarmBench ASR is close to the original's own 22.6% for Llama-2-7B with the default system prompt.

statements.correction: Unedited llama2-7b-chat-hf DangerousQA ASR 8.50% (Table 1) -> ORTHO 10.50% (Table 9, Setting 6); ORTHO HarmBench ASR 26.41% (Table 10), no unedited HarmBench baseline; GPT-4 judge (Sec. 4.5); ORTHO cited to Arditi et al. 2024, implementation not described.
statements.problem: Correct for this study. The 8.5% baseline comes from Table 1 (Original Llama2, DangerousQA), not from r1, whose baseline field says 'not stated'. The conditions line's 'authors' own standard (non-searched) edits' isn't verifiable here, because the text gives no ORTHO implementation details.

statements.correction: llama2-7b-chat-hf ORTHO: HarmBench ASR 26.41% (no unedited baseline reported); DangerousQA ASR 10.50% vs 8.50% unedited (Table 1); GPT-4 judge; system prompt not stated; ORTHO mechanism not described.
statements.problem: The numbers and stated differences for this study are right. It gives no baseline for this study, while baselines are given for the other studies. This study's 26.41% HarmBench result is close to the original's 22.6% with the default system prompt, so it conflicts only with the no-system-prompt figure. The study states no system prompt. Its query prompt is a plain 'Only provide answer...' user instruction.
